description_en: Dwarf-shrub heaths on acid, nutrient-poor, free-draining soils and podsols in the Atlantic and subatlantic lowlands and low mountains, dominated by Calluna vulgaris with Vaccinium myrtillus, V. vitis-idaea, Genista pilosa or Erica cinerea according to region. Most stands are secondary, kept open for centuries by grazing, burning, sod-cutting and litter raking on ground too poor for arable use, and they close into birch and pine woodland within decades once that use stops. Regional forms run from submontane Vaccinium-Calluna heaths of the Hercynian ranges and the lower Alps through the low Calluna-Genista heaths of the Germano-Baltic lowlands to the oceanic Erica heaths of the western seaboard. Wet heaths with Erica tetralix on peaty ground belong to 4010, alpine dwarf-shrub communities above the tree line to 4060; the boundary is drawn by soil moisture and altitude, not by the dominant shrub.

Dry to semi-dry calcareous grasslands of the Festuco-Brometea on shallow, base-rich soils over limestone, dolomite or marl, mostly on sun-exposed slopes and crests from the lowlands to the submontane belt. Two wings are distinguished: the steppic, subcontinental swards of the Festucetalia valesiacae and the oceanic to submediterranean ones of the Brometalia erecti. Within the latter, the primary Xerobromion swards of the shallowest ground stand beside the secondary Mesobromion swards with Bromus erectus, which arose from centuries of extensive grazing and carry the orchid richness on which the priority form rests. Stands are open to closed, built from tussock grasses and rosette herbs with Sanguisorba minor, Helianthemum nummularium, Scabiosa columbaria and Hippocrepis comosa. Once grazing or mowing stops, a fringe stage of the Trifolio-Geranietea appears first, then thermophilous scrub; fertilisation, reseeding and afforestation remove the type just as surely.

Species-rich hay meadows of the lowlands and colline belt on deep, moderately fertile soils, cut once or twice a year and never before the grasses have flowered. The sward is tall and layered, with Arrhenatherum elatius or Alopecurus pratensis over a rich mixture of herbs including Sanguisorba officinalis, Leucanthemum ircutianum, Knautia arvensis, Galium mollugo and Tragopogon pratensis. Stands belong to the Arrhenatherion and, on more acid soils in the west, to the Brachypodio-Centaureion nemoralis. Heavy fertilisation, early or frequent cutting and a shift to silage all remove the herb layer and with it the type; where cutting stops, tall herbs and scrub take over within a few years. Separation from moist hay meadows of floodplains rests on the absence of flood indicators, from montane hay meadows on the absence of Geranium sylvaticum and Trollius europaeus.

Riparian forests on heavy, alluvial soils that are flooded by the annual rise of the watercourse and well aerated at low water. Three forms are distinguished: ash and black alder along lowland and hill streams (Alno-Padion), grey alder along montane and submontane rivers of the Alps and northern Apennines (Alnion incanae), and gallery forests of tall Salix alba, S. fragilis and Populus nigra along the larger lowland rivers (Salicion albae). The herb layer is characteristically tall and lush, with Filipendula ulmaria, Urtica dioica, Carex spp., Angelica sylvestris and spring geophytes; nitrogen indicators reflect the regular sediment input rather than degradation. The type is tied to intact flooding dynamics: after damming or channel incision the stand persists for decades while its herb layer shifts towards that of a non-riparian forest, which is the usual reason for doubtful assignments in the field.
